claims.text: The initial Mg-containing alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
Mg is initially distributed uniformly throughout the matrix.
High-temperature exposure triggers preferential diffusion of Mg.
Preferential Mg diffusion causes Mg-rich intermetallic compounds to nucleate and grow.
Mg segregates preferentially to grain boundaries and defect clusters at service temperatures.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form especially at grain boundaries and defect sites.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases oxidize to form discrete patches of MgO.
Discrete MgO patches fail to coalesce into a continuous protective oxide barrier.
Discontinuous oxide formation caused by the intermetallics degrades corrosion resistance.
Discontinuous oxide formation caused by the intermetallics degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The initial homogeneous metastable solid solution transiently forms a continuous protective oxide film during short-term exposure.
Prolonged exposure will produce coarsened Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates relative to the initial state.
Prolonged exposure will produce discontinuous, patchy surface MgO relative to the initial state.
The exposed standard alloy will exhibit higher corrosion current density and inferior oxidation performance.
Suppressing Mg mobility will improve retention of a continuous protective oxide film and improve performance under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism is relevant during cyclic or prolonged exposure in air at 800–1100 °C.
Oxygen partial pressure and thermal cycling stress the integrity of the oxide film in this service regime.
The kinetics of Mg diffusion and the critical precipitate size or volume fraction needed to disrupt oxide continuity remain insufficiently quantified.
